questions.q: What is a block in a joined report?
options: A locked filter that users cannot change
A mini report with its own report type, columns, and filters
A dashboard component
A permission that stops sharing
questions.explain: A joined report is a set of blocks. Each block can have its own report type, columns, and filters.

questions.q: What lines up the rows across blocks in a joined report?
options: The record Id
The order in which blocks were created
Blocks are never lined up
A common grouping field shared by all blocks
questions.explain: Blocks align on a common grouping, such as Account Name or Priority. Report types with no shared field cannot be combined.

questions.q: Which is the best description of how a joined report differs from a SQL JOIN?
options: Each block runs as its own query and results are lined up by a shared grouping
It always returns a single merged result set
It only works on one object at a time
It cannot use filters
questions.explain: A joined report is like running separate queries and placing the results side by side keyed on a common field, not one merged JOIN.

questions.q: Which limitation is commonly true of joined reports in most orgs?
options: They cannot have filters
They can only contain a single record
They allow up to 5 blocks and are restricted as dashboard sources
They cannot be saved
questions.explain: Joined reports typically allow up to five blocks, and in most orgs they cannot be used as a normal dashboard source.

questions.q: Which scenario is the best fit for a joined report?
options: A simple list of contacts to export
A pie chart on a dashboard of opportunities by stage
Counting all opportunities in the org
Closed, new, and escalated cases compared by priority in one view
questions.explain: Joined reports shine when you compare separately filtered populations side by side. Lists and dashboard charts are better served by other formats.
